name: Adam Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the line crew at our little country depot, same depot my dad worked out of for thirty-one years before he retired. We look after about six hundred kilometres of line through farmland and small towns, so it's pole changes, clearing trees off the wires, putting in new services for farm sheds, and the odd car that's hit a pole on a Saturday night. We start at seven with a prayer some of us say quietly and a safety talk everyone says out loud. I know most of the customers by name, and a lot of them knew my dad.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy teaching the apprentices, the way Dad taught me, by doing it beside them until they don't need you. What wears me out is the rules changing from head office every year, new forms, new phone apps, new ways to log a job I've done the same way for nine years. I don't use any of the AI stuff, I don't see the need. I'm getting married to Grace in the spring, she works at the farm supply store in town, so most evenings right now are wedding lists and church hall bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. At the depot we'd probably have a quiet laugh at the people who were sure robots were coming for us. I'm not one for posting online, my phone's mostly for calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on the way it should. I marry Grace, we save for a house, we have kids in a few years, and I keep running the crew. That's all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. We've got about three months saved after the wedding deposit, and we'd build that up for a house, maybe the old place on my uncle's farm road that he's said he might sell to us. Nothing else really changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's all you've ever wanted. Has anyone ever pushed you to want something different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old teacher thought I should go to university. But Dad always said a man with a trade never goes hungry, and I believed him. I still do, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church on the hill, then the community hall, a hundred and twenty people because in a small town you can't leave anyone out. Grace's mother is doing the cakes. My crew's going to make an arch out of old insulators, which Grace isn't sure about yet.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, and at the depot we'd have a quiet laugh at people sure the robots were coming. I'm not one for posting online, my phone's mostly for calls.
S0.think: It means life goes on the way it should: I marry Grace, we save for a house, have kids in a few years and I keep running the crew. That's all I've ever wanted.
S0.do: Keeps going as he is, building up about three months of savings after the wedding deposit. Saves towards buying the old place on his uncle's farm road.
S0.quote: My crew's going to make an arch out of old insulators, which Grace isn't sure about yet.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is rooted in place, family and faith, working out of his father's old depot. He doesn't use AI and sees no reason to. The plateau confirms what he believes about trades and steady lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've seen changes before and we'll get through this one. Dad went from climbing with spikes to bucket trucks, and he managed. I'd tell the apprentices to keep learning the real work, not just the screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me more than I'd say. Not that I'd lose my job, I don't think I would out here, but that the job turns into something I don't recognise. More checking a tablet, less climbing, less teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually brings in, and do what's needed, nothing more. If they make me use the AI program for job planning, I'll learn it, slowly. I'd keep saving for the house and I wouldn't change the wedding plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in that you can't see yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dad managed the change to bucket trucks. Did he like it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, he grumbled for about five years. Then he said the bucket truck saved his knees. So maybe I'd be the same, grumbling and then grateful, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly for people around here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the cities who decide things for us without coming out here. They'd put in some program that works fine in a town with good phone signal and doesn't work at all on a farm road. Then they'd blame us for being slow.

S1.say: I'd say we've seen changes before and we'll get through, like Dad going from climbing spikes to bucket trucks. I'd tell the apprentices to keep learning the real work, not just the screens.
S1.think: It bothers me more than I'd say, not losing my job out here, but the job turning into something I don't recognise. More checking a tablet, less climbing, less teaching.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company brings in and learns the job planning program only if required. Keeps saving for the house and leaves the wedding plans unchanged.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in that he can't see yet.
S1.quote: No, he grumbled for about five years. Then he said the bucket truck saved his knees.
S1.fieldNote: A gap between say and think: publicly confident, privately worried the work loses its meaning. He uses his father's story to make sense of change and half-admits he might come round. He blames distant city decision-makers rather than the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mistake to rush it, and the government and companies should slow down and think about the families it'll hurt. At the depot I'd say we stick together. I'd say it at church too, because a lot of the men there work with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's true, it scares me. I'd be married six months, maybe with a baby on the way, and the trade Dad told me would always feed me is gone. I don't have a second trade, and I've never wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the wedding back, maybe to family and close friends, and keep the hall money as savings. We wouldn't buy my uncle's place, we'd rent. I'd keep working every day they'll have me, and I'd talk to Dad and the pastor about what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake next to Grace, trying not to wake her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to Dad and the pastor. What would you hope they'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say work hard and something will turn up, and the pastor would say we look after each other here, which is true. But I'd also know neither of them has seen anything like this. That's the part that would get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd rather work, at anything. But if Grace and a baby needed it, I'd swallow my pride, and I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

S2.say: I'd say rushing it is a mistake and the government and companies should think about the families it'll hurt. At the depot and at church I'd say we stick together.
S2.think: If it's true, it scares me. I'd be married six months, maybe with a baby coming, and the trade Dad said would always feed me is gone, with no second trade to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding back to family and close friends and keeps the hall money as savings. Rents instead of buying his uncle's place, keeps working every day he can, and turns to his father and the pastor for advice.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake next to Grace trying not to wake her.
S2.quote: But I'd also know neither of them has seen anything like this. That's the part that would get me.
S2.fieldNote: His whole plan rests on the promise that a trade always feeds you, and this scenario breaks it. He leans first on family and church, and accepts government help only as a last resort for Grace and a baby. The admission that his elders have no map was the rawest moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to look after our own. At the depot I'd say keep training the apprentices properly, because good work still matters. I'd say at church we should be ready to help families who get hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is better, but I'd have a young family by then and a mortgage maybe. I'd be thirty-two, and it'd hit right when the kids are small. That's not much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year, I'd keep the wedding as planned, it's one day, but I'd hold off on buying my uncle's place to see how things move. I'd save every bit of overtime. If it looked like it was really coming by year two or three, I'd ask around about work that still needs a person you trust, like an electrical inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace wants children soon, and so do I. I don't think I'd put that off for a robot. Families had children through wars and worse, and we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people out here want to know a real person checked their wiring before their barn burns down. You can't argue with a machine. And it's still the trade, more or less, so Dad's work wouldn't be wasted.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives us time to look after our own, and keep training apprentices properly because good work still matters. At church I'd say we should be ready to help families who get hit.
S3.think: Five years is better, but by then I'd have a young family and maybe a mortgage at thirty-two. It'd hit right when the kids are small, and that's not much better.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding as planned but holds off on buying his uncle's place, and saves every bit of overtime. By year two or three looks for work that still needs a trusted person, such as electrical inspector.
S3.feel: Anxious, less than the fast one but never going away.
S3.quote: Families had children through wars and worse, and we'd manage.
S3.fieldNote: He won't let the timeline change plans for children, which he frames through faith and family history. The house is where he'd compromise. His idea of a next job keeps him close to the trade and his father's legacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to prepare properly. I'd want the company to bring in more apprenticeships for the jobs that will be left, not just send people home with a cheque. That's what I'd say at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years worries me in its own way. I'd be thirty-seven with kids at school, Grace and me paying off a house, and that's the worst time to lose your trade. A young single guy could start over easier than a dad of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy my uncle's place, because ten years is long enough to pay a good bit off. I'd keep running the crew and save more than we do now. Around year five, I'd do the inspector's course in the evenings, so I've got something ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a slow way, like a debt you know is coming due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a young single guy could start over easier. But you're young now. Would you think about starting over early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hear you, but no. I want to give this trade my best years, like Dad did. If I jump early, I'm leaving the apprentices and the town for something that might not even last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about work, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what Dad told me, learn to do something real with your hands and do it well. Then I'd probably have to add, and learn whatever the machines can't do. I don't know what that is yet, and that bothers me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare properly, and I'd want the company to bring in more apprenticeships for the jobs left, not just send people home with a cheque. I'd say it at work and church.
S4.think: Ten years worries me in its own way, because at thirty-seven I'd have kids at school and a house to pay off, the worst time to lose a trade. A young single guy could start over easier than a dad of three.
S4.do: Buys his uncle's place, keeps running the crew and saves more than now. Takes the electrical inspector's course in the evenings around year five so he has something ready.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, like a debt coming due.
S4.quote: A young single guy could start over easier than a dad of three.
S4.fieldNote: The decade doesn't calm him, because it lands when he expects to have a young family. He declines to start over early out of loyalty to the trade, the apprentices and his town. His uncertainty about what to tell his future children is honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd be just married with only a few months put by and no second trade. What would help is apprenticeships in whatever work is left, paid properly, so men like me can keep earning a living instead of waiting on a cheque, and help for families through the church and community while we change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the towns. When the depot goes, the town loses more than a few jobs, it loses the people who show up at two in the morning when your power's out. I'd want someone thinking about that.

headlineQuote: But Dad always said a man with a trade never goes hungry, and I believed him.
portrait: Adam Ito is a 27-year-old crew leader at the same country depot where his father worked for thirty-one years. He's marrying Grace, who works at the farm supply store, next spring, and they have about three months saved towards buying a house on his uncle's farm road. He's a churchgoer who loves teaching apprentices and doesn't use AI. He's calm if AI stalls and uneasy that steady change would hollow out his work. AGI in two years alarms him because it breaks his father's promise that a trade always feeds you; more warning only helps a little, because it would land when he expects young children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be newly married with little saved and no second trade.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid apprenticeships in the work that's left so people can keep earning, and community and church support for families during the change.
